4	**Class length:** 50 minutes
5	**Prerequisites:** high-school algebra

8	
9	By the end of this module students can:
10	
11	1. Explain what statistics is for and tell a population from a sample, and a parameter from a statistic.
12	2. Classify variables (categorical or numerical) and their level of measurement.
13	3. Describe how data are collected (observational study or experiment, sampling methods) and spot common biases.
14	4. Choose a suitable graph for a variable.
15	5. Calculate and interpret measures of centre (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, IQR, standard deviation).
16	6. Find outliers with the 1.5 × IQR rule, compute z-scores and use the 68–95–99.7 rule.
17	7. Explain why correlation does not imply causation.
18	
19	---
20	
21	## 1. Why statistics?
22	
23	- Statistics is the science of **collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data** in the presence of variation and uncertainty.
24	- Two branches:
25	  - **Descriptive statistics** summarise the data we have (tables, graphs, averages). Most of this module.
26	  - **Inferential statistics** use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty. Later modules.
27	- Everyday examples: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, A/B tests on websites.
28	- The three questions that structure this module:
29	  1. **Where do the data come from?** (populations, samples, study design)
30	  2. **What kind of data are they?** (types of variables)
31	  3. **What do the data say?** (graphs, centre, spread, shape)
32	
33	## 2. Two stories about data
34	
35	**John Snow, London, 1854.** During a cholera outbreak in Soho, Snow marked each death on a street map. The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle was removed. A simple picture of data pointed to the cause.
36	
37	**The Literary Digest poll, 1936.** The magazine mailed about 10 million ballots, drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists, and got about 2.4 million back. It predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin D. Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with about 61% of the popular vote and 46 of the 48 states. George Gallup, with a much smaller but better-chosen sample (about 50,000 people), correctly predicted Roosevelt's win.
38	
39	Takeaway: **a huge biased sample is worse than a small well-chosen one.** How data are collected matters more than how much there is.
40	
41	## 3. Population, sample, parameter, statistic
42	
43	- **Population**: the entire group we want to know about (e.g. all students at the university).
44	- **Sample**: the part of the population we actually collect data from (e.g. 200 students who answered a survey).
45	- **Parameter**: a number describing the population (usually unknown). Notation: population mean **μ**, population standard deviation **σ**.
46	- **Statistic**: a number computed from the sample, used to estimate the parameter. Notation: sample mean **x̄**, sample standard deviation **s**.
47	- Memory aid: **P**opulation – **P**arameter; **S**ample – **S**tatistic.
48	
49	## 4. Types of variables
50	
51	| Type | Subtype | What it is | Examples |
52	|---|---|---|---|
53	| Categorical | Nominal | categories with no order | blood type, favourite colour, country |
54	| Categorical | Ordinal | categories with a natural order | satisfaction (low/medium/high), year of study |
55	| Numerical | Discrete | counts, whole numbers | number of siblings, goals scored |
56	| Numerical | Continuous | measurements on a scale | height, time, temperature |
57	
58	Watch out: numbers are not always numerical data. A postcode or a student ID is categorical; averaging them means nothing.
59	
60	## 5. Levels of measurement
61	
62	| Level | Order? | Equal intervals? | True zero? | Example |
63	|---|---|---|---|---|
64	| Nominal | no | no | no | eye colour |
65	| Ordinal | yes | no | no | race finishing position |
66	| Interval | yes | yes | no | temperature in °C |
67	| Ratio | yes | yes | yes | weight, income, time |
68	
69	Why it matters: 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C (interval, no true zero), but 20 kg is twice 10 kg (ratio).
70	
71	## 6. Collecting data: observational studies and experiments
72	
73	- **Observational study**: researchers observe and measure without assigning treatments (e.g. surveying students about sleep and grades). It can show an association, but not cause and effect.
74	- **Experiment**: researchers **assign** treatments and compare outcomes. Good experiments use:
75	  - a **control group** for comparison,
76	  - **random assignment** to groups, so the groups are alike apart from the treatment,
77	  - a **placebo** where possible, and **blinding** (double-blind: neither subjects nor researchers know who got what).
78	- Only a well-designed randomised experiment can establish **cause and effect**.
79	
80	## 7. Sampling methods
81	
82	| Method | How it works | Example |
83	|---|---|---|
84	| Simple random sample | every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen | draw 100 student IDs at random |
85	| Stratified sample | split into groups (strata), take a random sample from each | 25 students from each year of study |
86	| Cluster sample | split into groups, randomly choose whole groups | randomly pick 5 lecture sections, survey everyone in them |
87	| Systematic sample | choose every k-th individual from a list after a random start | every 20th name on the class list |
88	| Convenience sample | whoever is easiest to reach (**not random; avoid**) | asking friends in the cafeteria |
89	
90	## 8. Bias: when samples mislead
91	
92	- **Selection bias**: the way the sample is chosen leaves out part of the population (the Literary Digest's phone and car lists left out poorer voters in 1936).
93	- **Non-response bias**: the people who don't respond differ from those who do.
94	- **Response bias**: the question wording or setting pushes people towards an answer ("Don't you agree that…?").
95	- **Voluntary response bias**: only people with strong opinions choose to take part (online polls, call-in shows).
96	- A bigger sample does **not** fix bias; it only makes a biased answer look more precise.
97	
98	## 9. Graphs: picking the right one
99	
100	| Data | Graph | What it shows |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| One categorical variable | bar chart (or pie chart) | counts or percentages per category |
103	| One numerical variable | histogram | shape of the distribution |
104	| One numerical variable | box plot | five-number summary and outliers |
105	| Two numerical variables | scatter plot | relationship (direction, form, strength) |
106	| A variable over time | line graph | trends |
107	
108	Rule: **always plot the data before computing anything.**
109	
110	**Anscombe's quartet (1973):** four small data sets (11 points each) with almost the same mean of x (9), mean of y (about 7.50), correlation (about 0.816) and regression line (y = 3 + 0.5x), yet completely different scatter plots: one straight-line cloud, one curve, one line with a single outlier, one vertical stack with one far point. Summary numbers can hide the story.
111	
112	## 10. Describing a distribution: shape, centre, spread
113	
114	Every description of a numerical variable covers:
115	
116	- **Shape**: symmetric, skewed right (long tail to the right, e.g. incomes), skewed left; one peak (unimodal) or two (bimodal).
117	- **Centre**: where the typical value is.
118	- **Spread**: how much values vary.
119	- **Unusual features**: outliers, gaps.
120	
121	## 11. Measures of centre
122	
123	- **Mean**: add the values and divide by how many. x̄ = Σx / n
124	- **Median**: the middle value of the ordered data (average of the two middle values if n is even).
125	- **Mode**: the most frequent value.
126	
127	**Worked example.** Commute times (minutes) for 10 students:
128	
129	> 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 27, 30, 76
130	
131	- Sum = 260, n = 10 → **mean = 26 minutes**
132	- Ordered middle values are 20 and 22 → **median = 21 minutes**
133	- **Mode = 15 minutes** (appears twice)
134	
135	Remove the 76-minute commute: the mean drops to about **20.4**, the median only to **20**.
136	
137	- The median is **resistant** to outliers; the mean is not.
138	- In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled above the median (mean > median); in a left-skewed one, below.
139	- Use the median for skewed data (house prices, incomes); the mean for roughly symmetric data.
140	
141	## 12. Measures of spread
142	
143	- **Range** = maximum − minimum. Commute example: 76 − 12 = **64 minutes**. Very sensitive to outliers.
144	- **Quartiles**: Q1 is the median of the lower half, Q3 the median of the upper half.
145	  Commute example: lower half 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 → **Q1 = 15**; upper half 22, 25, 27, 30, 76 → **Q3 = 27**.
146	- **Interquartile range (IQR)** = Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 15 = **12 minutes**: the spread of the middle 50%.
147	- **Standard deviation (s)**: roughly the typical distance of values from the mean.
148	
149	> s = √( Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) )
150	
151	  Commute example: variance ≈ 341.3, **s ≈ 18.5 minutes**. Without the 76-minute value, s ≈ 6.1: one outlier triples the SD.
152	- We divide by n − 1 (not n) for a sample; this corrects for the sample mean being closer to the data than the true mean.
153	
154	## 13. The five-number summary, box plots and outliers
155	
156	- **Five-number summary**: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
157	  Commute example: 12, 15, 21, 27, 76.
158	- **1.5 × IQR rule** for outliers: a value is a suspected outlier if it is below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
159	  Commute example: 1.5 × 12 = 18; fences are 15 − 18 = **−3** and 27 + 18 = **45**. The **76-minute commute is an outlier**.
160	- A **box plot** draws the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values that are not outliers (here 12 and 30), and outliers as separate dots (here 76).
161	
162	## 14. z-scores: how unusual is a value?
163	
164	> z = (x − mean) / standard deviation
165	
166	- A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is above (+) or below (−) the mean.
167	- Example: an exam has mean 70 and SD 8. A score of 86 has z = (86 − 70) / 8 = **2**: two SDs above the mean.
168	- z-scores let us compare values on different scales (e.g. a score on a hard test vs an easy one).
169	
170	## 15. The 68–95–99.7 rule
171	
172	For data with a roughly **normal (bell-shaped)** distribution:
173	
174	- about **68%** of values lie within 1 SD of the mean,
175	- about **95%** within 2 SDs,
176	- about **99.7%** within 3 SDs.
177	
178	Exam example (mean 70, SD 8): about 68% of scores between **62 and 78**, about 95% between **54 and 86**, about 99.7% between **46 and 94**. A score of 86 (z = 2) is better than about 97.5% of the class.
179	
180	The rule only applies to roughly bell-shaped data; it does not apply to strongly skewed data like the commute times.
181	
182	## 16. Correlation is not causation
183	
184	- Two variables are **associated** (correlated) when they tend to move together.
185	- Classic example: across a year, **ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together**. Ice cream does not cause drowning; **hot weather** drives both. Hot weather is a **confounding variable**.
186	- Other reasons for a correlation without causation: reverse causation, coincidence (especially when many variables are searched).
187	- Only a randomised experiment (Section 6) can show cause and effect.
188	
189	## 17. Summary
190	
191	1. Statistics turns data into conclusions in the presence of variation.
192	2. Population → parameter (μ, σ); sample → statistic (x̄, s).
193	3. Variables are categorical (nominal, ordinal) or numerical (discrete, continuous).
194	4. How data are collected matters most: random sampling and randomised experiments; bigger biased samples do not help (Literary Digest 1936).
195	5. Always plot first (Anscombe's quartet).
196	6. Centre: mean (sensitive) vs median (resistant). Spread: range, IQR, SD.
197	7. Outliers: beyond Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
198	8. z = (x − mean) / SD; for bell-shaped data, 68–95–99.7.
199	9. Correlation is not causation; look for confounders.
200	
201	**Next module (Module 2):** Probability — the language of uncertainty.
202	
203	## 18. Check your understanding (quiz)
204	
205	1. Is "favourite colour" categorical or numerical, and at what level? *(Answer: categorical, nominal)*
206	2. A survey about exercise habits only asks people leaving a gym. What is the problem? *(Answer: selection bias from a convenience sample; gym-goers exercise more than the population)*
207	3. Find the mean and median of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10. *(Answer: mean 5, median 4)*
208	4. Which is resistant to outliers: the mean or the median? *(Answer: the median)*
209	5. An exam has mean 70 and SD 8. What is the z-score of 82? *(Answer: 1.5)*
210	6. Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated. Does ice cream cause drowning? *(Answer: no; hot weather is a confounding variable)*
211	
212	## Glossary
213	
214	- **Bias** — a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth in one direction.
215	- **Confounding variable** — a third variable that affects both variables being studied.
216	- **IQR** — interquartile range, Q3 − Q1.
217	- **Outlier** — a value far from the rest of the data.
218	- **Parameter** — a number describing a population.
219	- **Statistic** — a number computed from a sample.
220	- **Standard deviation** — a measure of the typical distance of values from the mean.
221	- **z-score** — the number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean.

  - a **control group** for comparison,

| Method | How it works | Example |
|---|---|---|

## 9. Graphs: picking the right one

| Data | Graph | What it shows |
|---|---|---|

- **Mode**: the most frequent value.

## 12. Measures of spread

- **Interquartile range (IQR)** = Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 15 = **12 minutes**: the spread of the middle 50%.
- **Standard deviation (s)**: roughly the typical distance of values from the mean.

## 13. The five-number summary, box plots and outliers

  Commute example: 12, 15, 21, 27, 76.
- **1.5 × IQR rule** for outliers: a value is a suspected outlier if it is below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
  Commute example: 1.5 × 12 = 18; fences are 15 − 18 = **−3** and 27 + 18 = **45**. The **76-minute commute is an outlier**.

## 14. z-scores: how unusual is a value?

> z = (x − mean) / standard deviation

- A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is above (+) or below (−) the mean.
- Example: an exam has mean 70 and SD 8. A score of 86 has z = (86 − 70) / 8 = **2**: two SDs above the mean.

## 15. The 68–95–99.7 rule

- about **68%** of values lie within 1 SD of the mean,
- about **95%** within 2 SDs,
- about **99.7%** within 3 SDs.

The rule only applies to roughly bell-shaped data; it does not apply to strongly skewed data like the commute times.

## 16. Correlation is not causation

- Two variables are **associated** (correlated) when they tend to move together.
- Classic example: across a year, **ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together**. Ice cream does not cause drowning; **hot weather** drives both. Hot weather is a **confounding variable**.
- Other reasons for a correlation without causation: reverse causation, coincidence (especially when many variables are searched).
- Only a randomised experiment (Section 6) can show cause and effect.

## 17. Summary

1. Statistics turns data into conclusions in the presence of variation.
2. Population → parameter (μ, σ); sample → statistic (x̄, s).
3. Variables are categorical (nominal, ordinal) or numerical (discrete, continuous).
4. How data are collected matters most: random sampling and randomised experiments; bigger biased samples do not help (Literary Digest 1936).
5. Always plot first (Anscombe's quartet).
6. Centre: mean (sensitive) vs median (resistant). Spread: range, IQR, SD.
7. Outliers: beyond Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
8. z = (x − mean) / SD; for bell-shaped data, 68–95–99.7.
9. Correlation is not causation; look for confounders.

**Next module (Module 2):** Probability — the language of uncertainty.

## 18. Check your understanding (quiz)

1. Is "favourite colour" categorical or numerical, and at what level? *(Answer: categorical, nominal)*
2. A survey about exercise habits only asks people leaving a gym. What is the problem? *(Answer: selection bias from a convenience sample; gym-goers exercise more than the population)*
3. Find the mean and median of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10. *(Answer: mean 5, median 4)*
4. Which is resistant to outliers: the mean or the median? *(Answer: the median)*
5. An exam has mean 70 and SD 8. What is the z-score of 82? *(Answer: 1.5)*

- **Outlier** — a value far from the rest of the data.

- **Statistic** — a number computed from a sample.
- **Standard deviation** — a measure of the typical distance of values from the mean.
- **z-score** — the number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean.

# The outline (PLAN.md)

The contract between planning and building. Whoever builds the deck follows it slide by slide, and the review compares the
finished deck against it, so every field is concrete: no "TBD" except facts the user still has to supply.

## Format

```markdown
# <Deck title>

- **Audience**: who, and what they already know
- **Occasion and time**: event, slot in minutes, whether Q&A is inside the slot
- **Goal**: what the audience should know, decide or do at the end
- **Promise**: By the end you will ... (said on slide 1 or 2)
- **Story**: the whole argument in one sentence
- **Fence**: what the idea is not (the nearest alternative it could be confused with)
- **Look**: data-theme, data-fonts (empty = the theme's own), lang/dir, one line on why
- **Sources**: each file or link used, one per line
- **Placeholders**: facts still missing, or "none"

| # | data-id | layout | claim (the slide's h2) | content and facts (with source) | role | min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | start | title | ... | subtitle = the promise | promise | 0.5 |
| 2 | agenda | agenda | ... | the parts | signpost | 0.5 |
| ... |
| n | close | closing | ... | what the audience now has, or the ask | contribution | 1 |

**Total**: n slides, about N minutes (finish at 85 to 90% of the slot when Q&A is inside it).
**Restatements of the story**: slides a, b, c (three, said three different ways).
```

## Rules for filling it in

- **Claim**: a sentence that states something ("Revenue grew 18%"), not a topic ("Revenue"). The titles alone, read in
  order, tell the story.
- **Content and facts**: only from the user's material, each with its source; anything missing is a named placeholder.
- **Role**, one or more per slide: promise, signpost, thesis (a restatement of the story), fence, evidence, story (an
  example or case that makes a number tangible), question (to the room), contribution, backup.
- **Layout**: one from `references/looks.md`; no more than two bullet slides in a row.
- **Minutes**: about one per slide for a talk, 1.5 to 2 for a lecture; the total fits the slot.
- **Required roles**: a promise in slides 1 to 2, the story restated three times, a fence, a contribution or the ask
  as the last slide (never "Thank you" or "Questions?"), and signposts when the talk is longer than about 10 minutes.
- Backup slides go last with role `backup`; they start with an appendix slide and are not counted in the time.

Don't add boxes around everything. ### keynote-black - **Overview.** Cinematic dark for reveals and demos; the same system on pure black. - **Colors.** bg `#000`, surface `#161618`, ink `#f5f5f7`, ink2 `#a1a1a6`, rule `#38383a`, brand `#2997ff`, em gradient `#2997ff` to `#c58bff`. - **Typography.** Inter 700 display; JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** 14 px radius, 6 px bars. - **Signature.** Gradient-filled headline accent, the only gradient in the system. Don't print it (use keynote-white for PDF handouts). ### boardroom - **Overview.** PowerPoint-corporate done well: navy, serif titles, gold accent, rules above the footer. - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#eef1f6`, ink `#0b2545`, ink2 `#46576f`, rule `#c8d0dc`, brand `#c19a3d` (text version `#7a5a0a`); hero bg navy `#0b2545` with gold `#e2b658`. - **Typography.** Source Serif 4 (600) titles, Source Sans 3 body, JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** 2 px radius, square bars, 1 px rules. - **Signature.** Gold spine on title and closing slides; gold left bar on every title; navy code panel. - **Do / Don't.** Do put the decision on the last slide. Builds, transitions, Magic Move **Builds** reveal parts of a slide one click at a time. Right arrow / space / click reveals the next build, then the next slide; left steps back. | Attribute | Effect | |---|---| | `data-build="fade"`, `rise`, `scale`, `wipe` | the element appears | | `data-build="list"` on a `ul`/`ol` | children appear one by one (`data-item="fade"` to change the style) | | `data-build="draw"` on an SVG shape or `<g>` | strokes draw themselves (every shape inside is staggered) | | `data-build="count"` | the number counts up from 0 (`$4.2M`, `38.4%`, `1,840` all work); markup holds the final value | | `data-build="draw"` on a chart figure | bars grow, lines draw, labels arrive | | `data-focus="1-3;5-7;*"` on a `pre` | each click lights the next range of lines (`*` = all) | | `data-order="2"` | builds with the same order arrive together; give all builds an order or none | | `data-delay="200"` | extra delay in ms | Print, overview thumbnails and `check.mjs` always show every build; the presenter window's Next pane shows the next one. Charts take `data-target="200"` (a dashed target line), `data-delta="pct"` or `"abs"` (a delta label on two-series columns), `data-muted="2"` (which series is the muted reference; with two bar series the second is one by default, `data-equal` turns that off) and `data-highlight` (also on line charts). Chart data is exposed to screen readers as a hidden table. Use builds where order matters; most slides need none. **Skip, appendix and the end.** `data-skip` on a slide keeps it in the overview, outline and PDF but jumps over it in play (Keynote's Skip Slide); use it for backup slides. A slide with `data-layout="appendix"` renders as a section divider and it and every slide after it are skipped in play. Pressing next on the last slide shows an "End of show" screen (`data-end="off"` on the deck turns it off). Cite sources with `<sup class="cite">[1]</sup>` and list them on a `references` slide (`<ol class="refs"><li><div><cite>Title</cite> <span>Detail</span></div></li></ol>`). Recipes: an agenda that returns at each section break, with `aria-current` on the current item; a Q&A slide is a `closing` slide whose label says Questions. **Transitions.** Default is a quick dissolve. `data-transition="push"`, `"move-in"` or `"none"` per slide (the incoming slide's setting wins). **Magic Move.** Give an element on one slide and an element on the next the same `data-magic="id"` and they morph: position, size, colour, opacity. If the typeface differs between the two (sentence to chip, serif to mono) it cross-fades while it travels. It works on text, boxes and SVG; use a `<span>` rather than `<em>` for text that changes colour. A slide pair with no shared ids just dissolves. ## 6. Diagrams that draw Author the SVG with `viewBox="0 0 1680 H"` (so 1 unit is 1 px at full width) and use the engine classes so it follows the theme: `dg-box` (outline), `dg-hot` (accent outline), `dg-line` and `dg-line hot`, `dg-dot`, text classes `dg-t` (label), `dg-s` (small), `dg-m` (mono), `dg-b` (accent). Wrap groups in `<g data-build="fade" data-order="1">` for boxes and `<g data-build="draw" data-order="2">` for arrows (stroke-only paths, arrowheads as part of the path). Crop the viewBox to the content (`viewBox="0 150 1680 330"`) so the diagram fills the slide. See `examples/src/gen_diagrams.py` for generators. ## 6b. Images Photos and illustrations go in `<img>` inside `image-left`, `image-right`, `team`, or as `data-bg` / `<img class="bleed">` on `full-bleed` (cropped with `object-fit: cover`, scrim added for legibility). Always give `alt` text. Re-encode photos without EXIF/GPS (Pillow: open, convert, save; `sips` alone keeps metadata). Local generation (nothing leaves the machine): `tools/gen-images.sh` renders the illustrations in `assets/` with the Draw Things CLI (`z_image_turbo`), strips metadata through Pillow and writes JPEGs of about 70 to 110 KB; `tools/gen-images.sh name "prompt" seed WxH` renders one more. Rules that came from the Wireless 101 pipeline: generated images are **illustrative only**; never ask for text, numbers, charts or diagrams (models garble them, so those stay SVG); no real people or brands; judge each render and drop the bad ones. STATS 101 · Module 1

Data, samples and describing data

By the end of this hour you can tell a sample from a population, pick a graph, and explain why correlation is not causation.

First-year course50 minutes

Welcome. This is an introductory course: you need only high-school algebra. Today's promise: you will be able to tell a population from a sample, classify variables, spot biased data, choose a graph, calculate and interpret centre and spread, find outliers and z-scores, and explain why correlation does not imply causation. Seven skills in fifty minutes, one idea at a time.

The plan

Three questions structure this hour

  1. Where do the data come from? populations, samples, study design
  2. What kind of data are they? types of variables
  3. What do the data say? graphs, centre, spread, shape

Every slide today answers one of these three questions. The label at the top of each slide tells you which. Learning objectives for the module: explain what statistics is for and tell population from sample, parameter from statistic; classify variables and levels of measurement; describe how data are collected and spot bias; choose a graph; calculate and interpret mean, median, mode, range, IQR and standard deviation; find outliers with the 1.5 x IQR rule, compute z-scores and use the 68-95-99.7 rule; and explain why correlation does not imply causation.

Statistics is the science of collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data.

Statistics works in the presence of variation and uncertainty: no two students have the same commute, and no sample is a perfect copy of the whole group. Three verbs to remember: collect, describe, conclude. Today is mostly the first two.

Where do the data come from?

Two branches: describe what we have, or infer beyond it

Descriptive statistics

Summarise the data we have: tables, graphs, averages. Most of this module.

Inferential statistics

Use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty. Later modules.

Fence: today is not about inference. Everyday examples of statistics: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, A/B tests on websites. Ask the room: which of these have you met this week? Descriptive statistics summarise; inferential statistics reach beyond the data in hand.

The magazine mailed about 10 million ballots, drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists, and got about 2.4 million back. It predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin D. Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with about 61% of the popular vote and 46 of the 48 states. Ask: with 2.4 million responses, what could possibly go wrong?

Takeaway

A huge biased sample is worse than a small well-chosen one

George Gallup, with a much smaller but better-chosen sample of about 50,000 people, correctly predicted Roosevelt's win. How data are collected matters more than how much there is.

Image placeholder: a 1936 newspaper front page about the Roosevelt landslide.

First statement of our main idea: how the data are collected matters more than how much there is. Gallup used about 50,000 people and got it right; the Digest used millions and got it wrong. Keep this in mind: we will return to it at the bias slide and in the summary.

Where do the data come from?

A sample gives a statistic that estimates the population's parameter

Population: the entire group we want to know about, for example all students at the university. Sample: the part we actually collect data from, for example 200 students who answered a survey. A parameter is a number describing the population, usually unknown, written mu for the mean and sigma for the standard deviation. A statistic is computed from the sample to estimate the parameter: x-bar for the mean, s for the standard deviation. Memory aid: P with P, S with S. Click through the four steps.

What kind of data are they?

Every variable is categorical or numerical

Categorical nominal: categories with no order, such as blood type, favourite colour, country. Categorical ordinal: categories with a natural order, such as satisfaction low, medium, high, or year of study. Numerical discrete: counts, whole numbers, such as number of siblings or goals scored. Numerical continuous: measurements on a scale, such as height, time, temperature. Watch out: numbers are not always numerical data. A postcode or student ID is categorical, and averaging them means nothing.

What kind of data are they?

Levels of measurement decide which arithmetic makes sense

LevelOrder?Equal intervals?True zero?Example
Nominalnononoeye colour
Ordinalyesnonorace finishing position
Intervalyesyesnotemperature in °C
Ratioyesyesyesweight, income, time

Why it matters: 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C, because temperature in Celsius is interval with no true zero. But 20 kg is twice 10 kg, because weight is ratio. Ask the room which row "year of study" would fall in; earlier we called it ordinal.

Where do the data come from?

Only an experiment can show cause and effect

Observational study

Researchers observe and measure without assigning treatments, e.g. surveying students about sleep and grades. It can show an association, but not cause and effect.

Experiment

Researchers assign treatments and compare outcomes. Only a well-designed randomised experiment can establish cause and effect.

The key word is assign. In the sleep and grades survey, nobody assigned sleep, so students who sleep more may differ in many other ways. In an experiment the researchers assign the treatments.

Where do the data come from?

A good experiment has four ingredients

  1. Control group

    for comparison

  2. Random assignment

    groups alike apart from the treatment

  3. Placebo

    where possible

  4. Blinding

    double-blind: neither subjects nor researchers know who got what

A control group gives the comparison. Random assignment to groups means the groups are alike apart from the treatment. A placebo is used where possible, and blinding goes further: in a double-blind experiment neither the subjects nor the researchers know who got what.

Where do the data come from?

Random sampling methods beat convenience

MethodHow it worksExample
Simple randomevery group of n individuals has the same chancedraw 100 student IDs at random
Stratifiedsplit into strata, random sample from each25 students from each year
Clustersplit into groups, randomly choose whole groupspick 5 lecture sections, survey everyone
Systematicevery k-th individual after a random startevery 20th name on the class list
Conveniencewhoever is easiest to reach: not random, avoidasking friends in the cafeteria

Four random methods and one to avoid. Simple random: every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen. Stratified: split into groups called strata and take a random sample from each. Cluster: split into groups and randomly choose whole groups. Systematic: choose every k-th individual from a list after a random start. Convenience: whoever is easiest to reach, not random, avoid.

Where do the data come from?

Four ways a sample can mislead

  • Selection bias. The way the sample is chosen leaves out part of the population.
  • Non-response bias. People who don't respond differ from those who do.
  • Response bias. Question wording or setting pushes people towards an answer.
  • Voluntary response bias. Only people with strong opinions take part.

Bias is a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth in one direction. Selection bias: the Literary Digest's phone and car lists left out poorer voters in 1936. Response bias example wording: "Don't you agree that...?" Voluntary response: online polls and call-in shows.

A bigger sample does not fix bias. It only makes a biased answer look more precise.

Second statement of the main idea, in different words: collection beats quantity. This is the Literary Digest lesson in one line. Fence: bigger is not automatically better.
